rationale: B wins by a nose because it turns the riskiest missing fact into the story instead of treating it as homework: "A profitable public company is scaling a circular shoe without saying what share actually gets recycled." A is very good, but its nearest equivalent, "On tests whether a circular shoe subscription can survive a public company's income statement," is a softer money-angle wrapper around the same absence of numbers. B has one shaky runner claim, but as strategy it gives the founder a clearer map of both press opportunity and reputational blast radius.
gaps_in_A: "On's nationwide Cyclon rollout is a commercial-scale test for castor-bean materials" overstates what the facts prove. Nationwide availability is not the same as meaningful material volume or supply-chain scale.
"take-back programs are widely seen as the operational graveyard of circular retail" is a strong line, but it imports an unsourced industry consensus not present in the update.
A leaves the best contrarian story in the proof drawer: "the recycling rate" appears as a required proof item, not as its own missing-denominator accountability angle.

"Meet the runner who never owns their shoes" is refused as hallucinated. Fair without a named subscriber, but too binary; a conditional pilot-subscriber or gear-review angle could work if On can produce the human.
gaps_in_B: "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" stretches one product launch into a trend. The angle needs volume, sourcing, or supplier evidence before it gets to say the feedstock is "becoming" anything.
"this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" is not in the facts. The return trigger is undisclosed, and B knows it because it later lists "the return trigger" as proof it needs.
"a pilot doesn't move a feedstock market, a national program might" is a useful hypothesis, not a grounded claim. Without unit volumes, it is trade-story bait with the hook only half tied.
